sections.skill: Explain why people save for retirement and how decades of compounding affect retirement savings

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Why do most people need their own retirement savings in addition to Social Security?

choices.text: Social Security pays each retiree twice their old salary
Retirement lasts only a few months for most people who retire
Employers pay workers forever after they retire
Social Security replaces only part of most workers' income

questions.correct_answer: Social Security replaces only part of most workers' income
questions.intro: Retirement can last 20 to 30 years or more. Social Security provides a monthly benefit, but for an average worker it replaces only about 40% of pre-retirement earnings. Most people need personal savings, often through workplace plans and IRAs, to cover the rest.
questions.feedback: Social Security covers only part of most people's needs in retirement.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: At 15, Ana invests $2,000 that earns an assumed 7% a year until she is 65 (50 years). About how much will it grow to?
questions.intro: Money invested for decades can grow far beyond what was put in, because growth compounds: A = P(1 + r)^t. (Real returns vary year to year and are not guaranteed.)
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Ben invests $6,000 a year for 40 years. At an assumed 7% a year, the account reaches about $1,197,811. How much of that is GROWTH rather than his contributions?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Lin earns $60,000 before retiring and wants 80% of that income in retirement. Social Security is expected to replace 40% of it. How much per year must come from savings?
questions.intro: A replacement goal is the share of pre-retirement income you want in retirement. Savings must fill the gap between that goal and other income such as Social Security.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which choice gives retirement savings the MOST time to compound?

choices.text: Waiting until age 50 to start saving
Starting contributions with a first job
Saving only in the final year before retiring
Waiting until debt is zero and a house is paid off

questions.correct_answer: Starting contributions with a first job
questions.feedback: Starting early gives the most years of compounding.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Retirement means living without a paycheck
sections.relationship: Students need to picture retirement as decades of expenses without wages before retirement accounts make sense.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: What is retirement?

choices.text: The years after a person stops working for pay

questions.correct_answer: The years after a person stops working for pay
questions.intro: Retirement is the stage of life after someone stops working full time. Without a paycheck, retirees live on savings, Social Security, and any pensions.
questions.feedback: Retirement is the period after paid work ends.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: If someone retires at 65 and lives to 90, how many years must their money last?
questions.intro: Years in retirement = age at death − age at retirement.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: A retiree spends $3,000 a month. How much is that per year?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which source of retirement income comes from the government?
questions.intro: Social Security is a federal program funded by payroll taxes. 401(k)s, IRAs, and brokerage accounts are savings the worker builds.
questions.feedback: Social Security is the government program.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Why does a 20-year-old have an advantage in saving for retirement?

choices.text: Young people can contribute more each year than older people
Decades of time for growth to compound
Retirement accounts pay higher interest rates to young savers
Young savers can take money out anytime without rules

questions.correct_answer: Decades of time for growth to compound
questions.feedback: Time is the young saver's biggest advantage.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Long-term retirement growth is exponential growth at a percent rate.

ref_skill.name: Recognize situations in which a quantity grows or decays by a constant percent rate per unit interval

sections.skill: Find a percent of a quantity
sections.relationship: Replacement goals and Social Security estimates are percents of income.

ref_skill.name: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: A common rule of thumb says a retiree might withdraw about 4% of savings in the first year. Using that rule, how much savings would provide $40,000 in the first year?
questions.intro: Rules of thumb, such as the "4% guideline," give rough targets: savings needed ≈ first-year withdrawal ÷ 0.04. They are estimates, not guarantees; market returns, inflation, and life span all matter.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Why is the 4% guideline only a rough estimate?

choices.text: It is a federal law for retirement accounts
It guarantees savings never run out
It applies only to people under 30
Future returns, inflation, and life span are uncertain

questions.correct_answer: Future returns, inflation, and life span are uncertain
questions.intro: Rules of thumb simplify complex questions. They are starting points for planning, not promises.
questions.feedback: Uncertain markets and longevity make any rule an approximation.

misconceptions.A: Mistakes a guideline for a rule

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: With prices rising 3% a year, about how much will $40,000 of today's spending cost in 24 years (Rule of 72)?
questions.intro: Inflation also compounds. At 3% a year, prices double in about 72 ÷ 3 = 24 years.
questions.feedback: At 3%, prices double in about 24 years: $40,000 → about $80,000.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Many planners suggest saving about 10–15% of income for retirement. On a $50,000 salary, what is 15%?
questions.intro: A savings rate is the percent of income saved: amount = income × rate.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which free tool helps estimate future Social Security benefits?

choices.text: A W-2 form from last year
A "my Social Security" account at ssa.gov
A retirement calculator on a bank's website

questions.correct_answer: A "my Social Security" account at ssa.gov
questions.intro: The Social Security Administration provides personalized benefit estimates through online accounts.
questions.feedback: SSA's online account shows earnings records and benefit estimates.

misconceptions.A: A pay stub shows withholding, not benefit estimates
misconceptions.B: Shows one year of wages, not projected benefits
misconceptions.D: Estimates savings, not the official benefit record

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: The cost of waiting to save for retirement

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Saver A invests $3,000 a year from 25 to 34, then stops. At an assumed 7%, the account is about $41,449 at 35 and about $442,537 at 70. How much did Saver A contribute?
questions.intro: Starting early, even for a few years, can produce more than saving much longer but starting later, because of extra years of compounding. (Examples assume a steady return; real returns vary.)
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Saver A contributed $30,000 and ended with about $442,537. What multiple of the contributions is that (nearest whole)?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which reason do young workers MOST often give for not saving for retirement?

choices.text: Retirement accounts are not allowed for workers under 30
Retirement feels far away compared with current needs
Employers do not let new workers join plans
Compounding works only for people who are already older

questions.correct_answer: Retirement feels far away compared with current needs
questions.intro: Present bias makes far-off goals feel less urgent. Automatic payroll contributions help overcome it.
questions.feedback: Present bias makes distant goals easy to postpone.

misconceptions.A: Believes there is a minimum age

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which feature helps overcome present bias in retirement saving?

choices.text: Saving only when they happen to remember

questions.intro: Automatic contributions happen without a new decision each payday.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Raising a 401(k) contribution by 1% of pay each year until it reaches a target is called…
questions.intro: Plan features: auto-enrollment signs workers up by default; automatic escalation raises the contribution rate a little each year; catch-up contributions let workers 50 and older save extra.

misconceptions.A: Confuses with extra contributions allowed at age 50+
misconceptions.C: Confuses with moving money between plans
misconceptions.D: Confuses raising the rate with investing on a schedule

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
